cognate: Arm. bok ~ ON berr (< *bʰosó-); Arm. het(i) ~ ON fótr (*ped-/*pod-)
drift_or_renewal: *bʰosó- is specialised to 'barefoot' by itself in Armenian and Balto-Slavic (Lith. basas, Serb. бос), whereas Germanic keeps 'bare' and needs the noun 'foot'; Armenian's added heti restores the foot-word
shared_syntax: motion verb + 'barefoot' adjunct (Arm. bok ew heti ... ertʻayin 'went barefoot and on foot'; ON gengom ... berom fótom 'we went with bare feet')
context: humiliation/supplication: Armenian noblewomen go barefoot to houses of prayer; ON townsmen surrender and go barefoot before the conqueror
phrase: *bʰosó- (pod-) 'go barefoot' as a mark of humility
note: Both texts Christian-era and the barefoot penitential gesture is a Christian commonplace; the ON passage may be translated. The point is lexical-semantic (specialisation of *bʰosó- to the feet in Arm. and BSl.) more than a poetic formula; Arm. bok < *bʰoso- is recalled from the literature.

cognate: Arm. owtem ~ Gk ἔδω; Arm. əmpem ~ Gk πίνω (also Hitt. ed-/eku- with renewed 'drink', Ved. ad-/pā-, Lat. edo/bibo)
shared_syntax: coordinated pair of verbs 'eat and drink' (Arm. owtē ew əmpē; Gk ἔσθειν καὶ πίνειν)
context: eating and drinking as the mark of mortal (living, dying) beings as opposed to gods/divine things: Yeghishe 'that which eats and drinks dies'; Od. 5.197 food 'such as mortal men eat' set before Odysseus, contrasted with Calypso's ambrosia (cf. Il. 5.341 gods neither eat bread nor drink wine, hence immortal)
phrase: *h₁ed- & *peh₃- 'eat and drink' merism, tied to mortality
note: Very common everyday pairing; Yeghishe's argument follows the biblical Bel and the Dragon topos ('does Bel eat and drink?'), so the Armenian is not independent evidence for a poetic formula; claimed only for the cognate merism with congruent mortal/immortal context.

search_lead.cognate: Arm. anown dnel 'give a name' (anown < *h₁nómn̥, dnem < *dʰeh₁-) ~ Gk ὄνομα θέσθαι ~ Ved. nā́ma dhā- (Hitt. lāman dai-, recalled)
search_lead.argument: Arm. zmec anown dnēr nma 'he set a great name on him' uses the inherited name-giving collocation *h₁nómn̥ dʰeh₁- with both members cognate; Greek and Vedic use it for naming persons (Arnaios' mother set his name; Autolycus asked to set the child's name). The 'great name' part is biblical (Gen. 12:2), but the name+put idiom is native Armenian. No partner in the slab bundle carries it.
